vignette:
She is 27 years old, Latin American, and works as an HVAC technician, a job she once liked for its rhythm and the satisfaction of solving problems with her hands. Before the trauma, she describes herself as practical, steady, and comfortable moving between apartments, rooftops, and mechanical rooms. She was the one who could crawl into tight spaces, lift heavy units, and keep her mind focused on what needed fixing. She had no intention of ever talking about what happened to her in detail, but over several sessions the story emerges in fragments, with long pauses where her body seems to remember before her words do.

Her trauma begins when she is taken and held by people who want information she does not have. What follows is a period she describes less as time and more as a sequence of sensations: the sting of restraints, the ache in her shoulders, the smell of sweat and metal, the sound of doors opening and closing somewhere nearby. She is interrogated repeatedly, threatened, deprived of sleep, and hurt in ways she still struggles to name directly. She says that during those days she learned to make herself very small inside her mind. If she could not stop what was happening, she tried to leave her thoughts somewhere else. At times she recites numbers or HVAC measurements to herself, anything mechanical and orderly, anything that cannot bleed.

After she is released, her life does not return to normal in the simple way other people seem to expect. She is physically out, but her body acts as though it is still braced for the next blow. In the first weeks, she startles at sudden noises and jerks around when a door slams or a coworker drops a tool behind her. She does not sleep for long stretches. When she does drift off, she wakes abruptly, convinced for a few seconds that someone is in the room. She keeps checking locks, windows, and the dark spaces behind doors. At home she leaves the television on because silence feels unsafe, yet the sound also keeps her on edge. She feels exposed in ways that are hard to explain, especially when she is alone.

Returning to work is both a relief and a challenge. HVAC allows her to move, climb, carry, and solve problems without needing to talk much, and she likes that. But she also notices that confined spaces now affect her differently. Attics, crawl spaces, and unfinished basements make her chest tighten. A service call in a building with a narrow utility room leaves her dizzy and sweaty, and she has to step outside before she can continue. Once, while crouched beside a broken compressor, she hears a chain rattle in the nearby mechanical room and goes instantly blank, unable to remember where she is for several seconds. She covers by saying she needs water, but afterward she trembles so hard she has to sit in her truck with both hands pressed against the steering wheel until her breathing slows.

She avoids reminders whenever she can. She stops watching crime reports and turns away when news stories mention detention, interrogation, or missing people. She no longer likes being touched unexpectedly, even in harmless ways. Friends say she seems distant. She misses social plans, then feels guilty and makes excuses about being tired from work. In crowds she scans exits without meaning to. In private she sometimes becomes angry in a flash, then ashamed of how fast it comes. On other days she feels numb, as if the life she is living belongs to someone who only resembles her. She says she is not sad all the time so much as cut off from feeling most things, and that includes the good ones.

There are moments when the memories break through with alarming force. A smell, a voice with a certain tone, or the scrape of metal can pull her back so completely that she sees the room where she was held as if it is happening again. She can feel the restraints, taste the dry fear in her mouth, and she has to look around and name objects in the present to convince herself she is here. Other times the memories arrive as fragments at night: a flash of light, a boot on the floor, her own voice begging someone to stop. She wakes with her heart pounding, drenched in sweat, and sometimes sits on the edge of the bed until dawn, listening to the building settle, trying to separate ordinary sounds from threat.

Even now, she continues to work and manage the basics of her life, but she does so with a vigilance that exhausts her. She describes herself as always waiting for something bad to happen, even on ordinary days. At the same time, there is a determined part of her that still shows up, still climbs the ladder, still repairs the system, still keeps moving.
